# Descriptive Analytics

## When Demand Happens

Taxi demand in Chicago follows predictable rhythms tied to work schedules, social activity, and weather.
Understanding those rhythms is the starting point for fleet positioning and driver scheduling.

![Pickup demand heatmap cross-tabulated by hour of day and day of week.](../data/raw/heatmap_hour_dow.png){width=80% fig-align="center"}

Weekdays are bimodal: a morning commuter peak around 08:00 and a stronger, broader evening peak between 16:00 and 19:00, with Tuesday to Thursday carrying the highest volumes in the dataset.
Weekends run on a different clock.
Demand starts later, builds gradually through the afternoon, and shows no commuter spike, because this is leisure travel.
The 00:00--06:00 window is uniformly quiet on every day of the week, which makes it the natural slot for charging and maintenance in an electric fleet.

Individual trips are short urban hops: median duration around ten minutes, most trips under five miles, and fares to match, with a long tail from airport and cross-city rides (distributions in @sec-app-figures).
Idle time between a driver's consecutive trips concentrates in the 0--30 minute range, though a mean near an hour points to periods of deliberate waiting or repositioning.

## Where Demand Happens

To analyse space consistently we discretise the city with Uber's H3 hexagonal grid, which offers uniform cell areas and clean adjacency where administrative boundaries don't (grid illustration in @sec-app-figures).
The maps below use resolution 7.
The forecasting models in Section 5 operate one step coarser, at resolution 6.

![Choropleth maps of pickup demand aggregated at community area level and H3 resolutions 6, 7, and 8.](../data/raw/demand_choropleth.png){width=80% fig-align="center"}

The Near North Side and the Loop dominate demand, consistent with their role as Chicago's central business and entertainment district, while O'Hare forms a structurally distinct cluster in the far northwest.
As resolution increases the hotspots sharpen into specific corridors (the Magnificent Mile, River North, the area around O'Hare), and areas that look moderate at community level turn out to vary strongly inside.
Community-area aggregation hides exactly the sub-neighbourhood differences a fleet needs for positioning decisions.

The picture shifts over the day, but the downtown-lakefront corridor stays dominant in every 4-hour window (maps in @sec-app-figures).
Overnight, the downtown core keeps relative activity from hospitality traffic.
Early mornings add a secondary hotspot around Midway from first departures, and the evening windows intensify the core sharply while the outskirts stay comparatively quiet.

## Flows Between Areas

Where trips go matters as much as where they start.
The origin--destination analysis (matrix in @sec-app-figures) shows the Near North Side and the Loop dominating as both origins and destinations.
O'Hare, despite its distance, sends nearly 500,000 trips toward those two areas alone, making the airport-to-downtown corridor one of the most dependable sources of paid mileage in the network.
Vehicles dropping passengers in outer neighbourhoods, by contrast, face a structural repositioning problem to get back to demand.

Net flow, defined as pickups minus dropoffs per hexagon, turns that imbalance into something a planner can act on: persistently positive cells need more vehicles than dropoffs return, and negative cells accumulate them.

![Net flow (pickups minus dropoffs) by H3 hexagon, aggregated across the full observation period.](../data/raw/netflow_4h_buckets.png){width=80% fig-align="center"}

The downtown core and the O'Hare corridor consistently hand out more trips than they take back, while the residential outskirts act as vehicle sinks.
For an electric fleet this points straight at infrastructure: chargers placed in the negative-flow residential zones turn otherwise idle accumulation into productive charging time, before vehicles are repositioned to the high-demand corridors.
